"The visit focused on strengthening relations between the two countries and on regional challenges," the official statement read, adding that Netanyahu was accompanied by the head of the National Security Council, the head of the Mossad, the military secretary and the foreign policy adviser.

Iran, notably, is itself a neighbour to both Turkey and Pakistan. Yet while none of these states is a direct party to the war on Iran, all three are nevertheless fighting on two fronts at once: an economic front at sea, and a security one on land.
The logic is straightforward. Insurers price in the risk of a tanker being struck near Hormuz, where Iran retains significant leverage over passage. And Suez, one of Egypt’s most reliable sources of foreign currency, has seen its revenues collapse by more than 60 percent.
None of these countries needed a new war to hurt. Pakistan’s inflation had already hit a record 38 percent in 2023, with reserves barely covering two weeks of imports. On Friday, oil prices fell amid news of an Iranian proposal and optimism after the UN General Assembly. However, prices bounced back at the start of the new week, with Brent back above $106 a barrel.
Despite rejecting the offer, Trump told Axios he expects negotiations to resume, but added that Tehran "overplayed their hand".
"They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make... It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago."

The order followed Erdogan’s announcement that Turkey had asked Interpol to issue a red notice for Netanyahu, the report said.
Israel could itself seek to bring the case before the International Criminal Court in The Hague, which issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu in 2024 on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity allegedly committed in Gaza since October 2023.

The report follows Netanyahu’s speech to the UN General Assembly on Friday, in which he called Erdogan a “tyrant”.

Meshaal said the measures included the reported 40-day closure of the mosque, what he described as the “imposition of temporal division” to facilitate incursions by “extremist Jewish groups” and efforts to create “spatial division” by emptying key facilities within the courtyard, according to a statement.
Al-Aqsa “stands at a crossroads”, Meshaal said, and called for steps to protect the site, including what he called a “strategy of resistance and jihad”.
He also urged Arab and Muslim-majority countries to back Palestine and called on Palestinians to keep a “steadfast presence” at the mosque.
The comments come a week after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu toured tunnels beneath Al-Aqsa Mosque as hundreds of Israeli settlers raided the Jerusalem holy site.
Netanyahu joined tens of thousands of Israelis for Selichot prayers at the Western Wall, adjacent to Al-Aqsa, ahead of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.
The prime minister later posted a video of himself and his wife, Sara, touring tunnels beneath the Al-Aqsa Mosque complex.
“It is moving to touch the rock of our existence. We are here very close to the Holy of Holies,” he said. “We are here, and we will always remain here.”
On 20 September, hundreds of Israelis raided Al-Aqsa, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir.

Israeli forces have tightened restrictions around the occupied West Bank city of Ramallah, closing roads and entrances to several towns and villages, Wafa news agency reported.
The development comes after Israeli authorities decided to impose a “comprehensive closure” on the occupied West Bank and close crossings into the territory until Saturday for the Jewish holiday of Sukkot.
Local sources told the agency that the entrance gate to Turmus Ayya, north of Ramallah, was closed and residents were “harassed”.
Wafa also reported that entrances to Aboud, Nabi Saleh, Atara and Taybeh were closed, while military checkpoints were set up at the entrances to Yabroud and Ein Sinyah.

'I'm a man of strong faith,' says Irish goalkeeper after withdrawing from Israel match
Republic of Ireland goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu has withdrawn from the team’s Nations League match against Israel, saying his decision was based on his opposition to the killing of civilians.
“My decision is based purely on the belief the killing of innocent people is wrong,” Bazunu said in a statement posted on social media.
“Representing my country means everything to me,” Bazunu wrote. “I am a man of strong faith and try my best to be a person of morals and principles, therefore I feel that participating in the upcoming matches against Israel would be wrong.”
He added: “There are times when you have the opportunity to stand for a greater cause, and I strongly believe this is one of those moments.”
The Republic of Ireland will nevertheless play Israel in Sunday's Uefa Nations League match in Debrecen, Hungary, after the squad voted by a significant majority to proceed with the fixture, Football Association of Ireland CEO David Courell said Saturday.
The vote followed several hours of discussions at the team hotel over whether to boycott the game.
Ireland will wear black armbands during the match and will not shake hands with the Israeli players before kickoff, according to the report.
